text: Farm records (កំណត់ត្រាកសិដ្ឋាន) help a smallholder see whether livestock are actually profitable, since a high sale price doesn't automatically mean high profit once feed, labor, veterinary costs, and transport are counted. Record number/type of animals, births/hatchings, deaths, purchases, sales, feed quantities and costs, veterinary expenses, vaccination dates, health problems, labor, and major equipment costs. For cattle: body condition, breeding, calving, illness, purchase/sale dates and prices. For pigs: litter size, piglet deaths, growth, feed use, finishing weight. For poultry, flock-level (not individual) records are usually realistic: starting number, deaths, feed cost, eggs collected/sold, birds sold, age at sale, price. Calculate net income = sales revenue minus major production and marketing costs, not just the sale price. Compare batches or seasons (e.g. a lower-priced but lower-cost batch can be more profitable than a higher-priced, higher-cost one) rather than assuming the highest sale price means the best outcome. Record wet-season and dry-season conditions separately -- e.g. 'heavy rain for several days; pen remained wet; feed consumption decreased' -- since this reveals real patterns rather than vague impressions. Records also function as an early-warning system: a sudden drop in egg production or feed intake deserves investigation. A paper notebook is sufficient -- do not require computerized systems, individual animal ID, or precise labor accounting from a smallholder. Never invent a breed, market price, or veterinary diagnosis the farmer hasn't provided; keep farmer observation, general knowledge, and professional diagnosis as three distinct levels.
